newsitem.title: USA: Circuit City's CarMax IPO starts with gains.
newsitem.headline: Circuit City's CarMax IPO starts with gains.

text.p: Wall Street investors snapped up shares of the CarMax Group on Tuesday, a day after the market debut of the Circuit City Stores Inc unit that sells used cars and trucks in superstores.

On their first day of trading, shares rose 1-1/8 to 21-1/8 from their IPO price of $20. More than nine million shares had been traded at midday, making it the most active stock on the New York Stock Exchange.

Cantor Fitzgerald IPO analyst Vince Slavin said the very large size of the offering -- which was raised to 21.86 milion from 18.86 million shares -- could hold down opening premiums and disguise strong demand from institutional investors.
The shares were priced at $20 each last night after lead underwriter Morgan Stanley & Co raised the estimated price for the deal, signaling strong demand.
Circuit City still owns about 80 percent of CarMax, which will remain a division of the consumer electronics retailer.

CarMax is aiming for the highly-fragmented and lucrative used car industry. It currently operates six stores in the Southeast United States and a vehicle reconditioning center in Orlando, Fla., which offer between 400 to 1,200 vehicles each. Prices are generally $500 to $1,000 below book value, defined by the National Automobile Dealers Association (NADA).

With the $400 million it will pocket from the IPO, CarMax plans to launch an ambitious expansion. Its prospectus said it plans to have 80 to 90 stores by the end of fiscal 2002, up from about a half dozen now.

Although CarMax has yet to turn a profit, the existing stores are showing strong early results with same-store sales gains of 22 percent in the third quarter of fiscal 1997, Natwest Markets retail analyst John McKenna said in a research report.

Another positive sign for the company is the willingness by big automakers, including Ford Motor Co and Chrysler Corp, to deal with auto superstores, the report said. That gives CarMax better access to vehicles and could give auto superstores access to new car sales, he said.

McKenna also said the $600 billion automotive retailing industry is a big enough sector to support competition. Wayne Huizenga, who proved he can consolidate and revolutionize an industry with Blockbuster Entertainment, has also set his sights on the used-car industry. His Republic Industries Inc owns AutoNation USA.

"We estimate that if the auto-superstores can capture just ten percent market share of the new and used auto market, the top 50 markets can support at least 350 to 400 auto-superstores," the report said.
